Thus  

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}a&a+r\\a+2r&a+3r\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
\det M =a(a+3r)-(a+r)(a+2r)= -\,2r^{2},
\qquad 
\operatorname{tr}M =2a+3r .
\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### When does a power of \(M\) belong again to \(S\) ?

For a \(2\times2\) matrix \(X=\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{pmatrix}\) the condition “its entries are an arithmetic progression’’ is equivalent to  

\[
2q=p+r,\qquad 2r=q+s .
\tag{3}
\]

Equivalently,
\(X\) satisfies \(X^{2}-(\operatorname{tr}X)X+(\det X)I_{2}=0\) (Cayley–Hamilton).  
If \(\operatorname{tr}X=0\) then (3) holds automatically, because
\(X^{2}+(\det X)I_{2}=0\) gives \(X^{2}=-(\det X)I_{2}\), a scalar matrix,
and a scalar matrix clearly satisfies (3).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Eigenvalue viewpoint

Let \(\lambda,\mu\) be the (real) eigenvalues of \(M\).  
From (2),

\[
\lambda+\mu =\operatorname{tr}M =2a+3r,\qquad 
\lambda\mu =\det M =-2r^{2}.
\]

If some power \(M^{k}\) (\(k>1\)) belongs to \(S\), then \(M^{k}\) must be a scalar
matrix (the only matrices of the 2‑dimensional subspace (3) that are powers of a given
non‑scalar matrix).  Hence \(\lambda^{k}=\mu^{k}\).
Because \(\lambda,\mu\) are real, the only possibilities are

* \(\lambda=\mu\) (the matrix is already a scalar multiple of the all‑ones matrix, i.e. \(r=0\));
* \(\lambda=-\mu\) (which forces \(\lambda+\mu=0\), i.e. \(\operatorname{tr}M=0\)).

No other real ratio can satisfy \((\lambda/\mu)^{k}=1\) for an integer \(k>1\).
